| Operator | Bitwise Operation | Example (`a = 5 (0101₂), b = 3 (0011₂)`) |
|---|---|---|
| `&` | **Bitwise AND** (`1` iff both bits are `1`) | `5 & 3 = 1` (`0001₂`) |
| `|` | **Bitwise OR** (`1` if either bit is `1`) | `5 | 3` -> `7` (`0111₂`) |
| `^` | **Bitwise XOR** (`1` iff bits differ) | `5 ^ 3 = 6` (`0110₂`) |

| `<<` | **Bitwise Left Shift** (shifts left; multiplies by `2ⁿ`) | `5 << 1 = 10` (`1010₂`) |
| `>>` | **Bitwise Right Shift** (shifts right; divides by `2ⁿ`) | `5 >> 1 = 2` (`0010₂`) |

**Structured programming** organizes software around top-down modular functions and three clean control structures (**sequence**, **selection**, **iteration**):

- **Modularity & Top-Down Decomposition:** Complex problems are broken into small, single-purpose functions that are easy to design and reason about.
- **Code Reusability:** Common routines are written once and called wherever needed without duplicating logic.
- **Eliminates Spaghetti Code:** Avoiding arbitrary `goto` jumps makes control flow predictable and readable.
- **Easier Debugging, Testing & Maintenance:** Individual modules can be developed in parallel and unit-tested or updated independently.

- **Classification Basis:** C user-defined functions are classified into **four categories** depending on whether **arguments are passed** and whether a **return value is sent back**:

| Category | Prototype Pattern | Data Flow |
|---|---|---|
| **1. No arguments & no return value** | `void greet(void);` | Neither sends inputs nor returns a result. |
| **2. Arguments & no return value** | `void printSum(int a, int b);` | One-way input from caller to callee; callee prints/acts directly. |
| **3. No arguments & returns a value** | `int readChoice(void);` | One-way output from callee back to caller via `return`. |
| **4. Arguments & returns a value** | `int add(int a, int b);` | Full two-way communication between caller and callee (most reusable). |

> [!TRAP] Strict ISO C Note vs Paper Left-to-Right Trace
> Under strict ISO C99/C11 rules, `c = a++ + --b - a++ + b;` invokes **Undefined Behaviour** because variable `a` is modified twice (`a++` and `a++`) between two adjacent sequence points without a defined evaluation order.

- **Conventional Left-to-Right Classroom Paper Trace (`a = 8, b = 4` initially):**
  1. First `a++` yields **`8`** (`a` becomes `9`).
  2. `--b` pre-decrements `b` to `3` and yields **`3`**.
  3. Second `a++` yields **`9`** (`a` becomes `10`).
  4. Final `b` reads current `b` = **`3`**.
  5. Substitute left-to-right: `c = 8 + 3 - 9 + 3 =` **`5`** (with final `a = 10`, `b = 3`, **`c = 5`**; note compilers that delay post-increments until `;` may yield `8 + 3 - 8 + 3 = 6`).

> [!COMPARE] Compiler vs Interpreter
> | Parameter | Compiler | Interpreter |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Translation Unit** | Scans and translates the **entire source program at once** before execution. | Translates and executes **one statement/line at a time**. |
> | **Output Artifact** | Produces a standalone relocatable/executable machine-code file (`.o`, `.exe`). | Produces **no standalone binary**; source is re-interpreted each run. |
> | **Execution Speed** | **Faster runtime execution** (native CPU instructions). | **Slower runtime execution** due to runtime translation overhead. |
> | **Error Reporting** | Reports **all syntax/type errors together** after scanning the whole file. | Stops immediately at the **first error encountered** during execution. |
> | **Language Examples** | C (`gcc`, `clang`), C++, Rust. | Classic Python, Ruby, shell scripts (`sh`). |

An **array** stores fixed-size homogeneous elements in contiguous memory and is classified into **three types** by the number of subscripts (dimensions):

- **1. One-Dimensional (1D / Linear) Array:** Uses a single index `type name[size];` to store a linear list (e.g., `int marks[5] = {78, 85, 90, 66, 82};`).
- **2. Two-Dimensional (2D / Matrix) Array:** Uses row and column indices `type name[rows][cols];` stored in **row-major order** to represent tables and matrices (e.g., `int mat[3][3];`).
- **3. Multi-Dimensional (3D+) Array:** Uses three or more subscripts `type name[d1][d2][d3];` (an array of 2D matrices, e.g., `int rgb[3][256][256];`).

> [!COMPARE] Source Code vs Object Code
> | Parameter | Source Code | Object Code |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Representation** | Human-readable high-level C statements written in plain ASCII/UTF-8 text. | Machine-oriented binary instructions and relocation metadata (`0`s and `1`s). |
> | **Created By** | Written and edited directly by the **programmer** in a text editor/IDE. | Generated automatically by the **compiler / assembler** from source code. |
> | **File Extension** | `.c` and `.h` files. | `.o` (Unix/Linux) or `.obj` (Windows) files. |
> | **Portability** | **Portable** across CPU architectures (can be recompiled anywhere). | **Architecture-specific** (bound to target CPU ISA such as x86-64 or ARM). |
> | **Direct Execution** | Cannot run directly; must be compiled and linked first. | Linked with library object files by the **linker** to form an executable. |

> [!MARKS] 4 + 4 = 8 Marks (`a`: Storage classes in C — 4m · `b`: Call by value vs call by address — 4m)

### Part (a) — Storage Classes Used in C

- **Role:** C's four variable storage classes specify **storage location**, **default initial value**, **scope/linkage**, and **lifetime**:

| Storage Class | Storage Location | Initial Value | Scope / Linkage | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `auto` | Stack (RAM) | Garbage | Local to block (no linkage) | Until block exits |
| `register` | CPU register (hint) | Garbage | Local to block (`&` illegal) | Until block exits |
| `static` | Data / BSS segment | `0` | Block-local or file-internal | Entire program execution |
| `extern` | Data / BSS segment | `0` | Global across `.c` source files | Entire program execution |

- **Example:** `static int count = 0; count++;` inside a function keeps its incremented value across calls, whereas `auto int count = 0;` resets on every invocation.

### Part (b) — Call by Value vs Call by Address

> [!COMPARE] Call by Value vs Call by Address in C
> | Parameter | Call by Value | Call by Address |
> |---|---|---|
> | **What Is Passed** | Copies of actual argument **values** (`swap(a, b)`). | Memory **addresses** of actual variables (`swap(&a, &b)`). |
> | **Formal Parameters** | Ordinary value variables (`int x, int y`). | Pointer variables (`int *x, int *y`). |
> | **Caller Side Effects** | Changes inside callee **never** alter caller variables. | Dereferencing `*x` directly updates caller variables in place. |
> | **Memory & Return** | Copies full data; returns only one scalar value. | Copies compact addresses; can update multiple caller outputs. |

```c
void byVal(int x)  { x = 50; }       /* caller variable unchanged */
void byAddr(int *p){ *p = 50; }      /* caller variable becomes 50 */
```

> [!MARKS] 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 Marks (`a`: `calloc()` vs `malloc()` — 3m · `b`: Recursion vs iteration — 2m · `c`: "Hello World" C program & header explanation — 3m)

### Part (a) — `malloc()` vs `calloc()` (`<stdlib.h>`)

> [!COMPARE] `malloc()` vs `calloc()` Dynamic Memory Allocation
> | Parameter | `malloc()` | `calloc()` |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Prototype & Arguments** | `void *malloc(size_t size)` — **1** argument (total bytes). | `void *calloc(size_t n, size_t size)` — **2** arguments (count, element size). |
> | **Memory Initialization** | Leaves allocated heap bytes **uninitialized** (garbage values). | Initializes every allocated byte to **zero (`0`)**. |
> | **Allocation Concept** | Single raw block of `size` bytes. | Contiguous array of `n` elements of `size` bytes each. |

### Part (b) — Recursion vs Iteration

> [!COMPARE] Recursion vs Iteration in C
> | Parameter | Recursion | Iteration |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Mechanism** | A function calls itself until a **base case** is reached. | Repeats a statement block using `for`, `while`, or `do-while`. |
> | **Stack & Speed** | Pushes a new stack frame per call (higher memory & call overhead). | Uses constant `O(1)` stack space and faster loop jumps. |
> | **Failure Mode** | Missing base case causes **stack overflow** crash. | Missing termination update causes an **infinite loop**. |

### Part (c) — Complete "Hello World" Program & Header Purpose

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hello World\n");
    return 0;
}
```

- **Purpose of `#include <stdio.h>`:** Includes the **Standard Input/Output header** during preprocessing, supplying the prototype `int printf(const char * restrict format, ...);` (along with `scanf`, `FILE`, `stdin`, `stdout`) so the compiler type-checks the `printf()` call before linking against the C standard library; `return 0;` signals successful exit status to the host OS.

> [!MARKS] 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 Marks (`a`: Header file vs library file — 2m · `b`: Operator precedence & associativity — 4m · `c`: `==` vs `=` — 2m)

### Part (a) — Relation Between Header File and Library File

- **Header File (`.h`):** A human-readable source file included during **preprocessing** (`#include <math.h>`) that supplies **declarations/interfaces**—function prototypes, `#define` macros, and type definitions—so the compiler can type-check calls.
- **Library File (`.a` / `.lib` / `.so` / `.dll`):** A pre-compiled binary archive joined during **linking** (`gcc prog.c -lm`) that contains the actual machine-code **definitions/bodies** of those standard functions (`sqrt()`, `printf()`).

### Part (b) — Operator Precedence and Associativity

- **Operator Precedence:** Determines **which operator binds first** when an unparenthesized expression contains operators from different priority tiers:
  - Example: In `int x = 2 + 3 * 4;`, `*` has higher precedence than `+`, so C evaluates `2 + (3 * 4) = 14` (not `20`).
- **Operator Associativity:** Resolves ties when adjacent operators belong to the **same precedence tier**:
  - **Left-to-Right (`*`, `/`, `%`, `+`, `-`):** `20 / 5 / 2` groups as `(20 / 5) / 2 = 4 / 2 = 2`.
  - **Right-to-Left (`=`, `+=`, unary `!`, `~`, `? :`):** `a = b = 10` groups as `a = (b = 10)`, assigning `10` to `b` and then `10` to `a`.

### Part (c) — Equality (`==`) vs Assignment (`=`) Operator

> [!COMPARE] Equality (`==`) vs Assignment (`=`) in C
> | Parameter | Equality Operator (`==`) | Assignment Operator (`=`) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Category & Purpose** | Relational operator testing whether two values are equal. | Assignment operator storing RHS value into LHS variable. |
> | **Side Effect** | Does **not** modify either operand (`5 == x` is legal). | Overwrites LHS lvalue (`5 = x` is a compile-time lvalue error). |
> | **Evaluated Result** | Yields integer `1` (true) or `0` (false). | Yields the assigned value stored in LHS (`if (x = 5)` is always true!). |

> [!MARKS] 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 Marks (`a`: Advantages of user-defined functions — 3m · `b`: Declaration vs definition — 2m · `c`: Actual vs formal parameters — 3m)

### Part (a) — Advantages of User-Defined Functions

- **Modularity (Top-Down Decomposition):** Breaks a large, complex program into smaller, single-responsibility sub-modules (`readData()`, `computeTax()`, `printReport()`), keeping `main()` concise.
- **Code Reusability:** Write logic once and invoke it from multiple places without duplicating lines of code.
- **Easier Debugging & Testing:** Bugs are isolated to individual functions whose inputs and outputs can be tested independently.
- **Team Collaboration & Maintainability:** Different programmers can implement separate functions simultaneously as long as prototypes are agreed upon.

### Part (b) — Function Declaration vs Function Definition

> [!COMPARE] Function Declaration (Prototype) vs Function Definition in C
> | Parameter | Function Declaration (Prototype) | Function Definition |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Purpose** | Tells the compiler the function's name, return type, and parameter types. | Supplies the actual executable statements (body) of the function. |
> | **Syntax & Semicolon** | Ends with a semicolon `;` and has no `{}` body: `int add(int, int);` | Followed by a compound `{ ... }` block with no header semicolon. |
> | **Memory Allocation** | Allocates **zero** machine-code storage; may appear multiple times. | Generates compiled code; must appear **exactly once** (One Definition Rule). |

### Part (c) — Actual Parameters and Formal Parameters with Example

- **Actual Parameters (Arguments):** Values, variables, or expressions passed inside parentheses at the **function call site** (`sum = add(num, 10);`).
- **Formal Parameters:** Local typed variables listed in the **function definition header** (`int add(int a, int b)`) that receive copies of the actual arguments upon invocation.

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int add(int a, int b) {         /* a, b = formal parameters */
    return a + b;
}
int main(void) {
    int x = 7;
    printf("%d\n", add(x, 5));  /* x, 5 = actual parameters -> prints 12 */
    return 0;
}
```

questions.answer:
> [!MARKS] 4 + 4 = 8 Marks (`a`: Four C storage classes with example — 4m · `b`: Call by Value vs Call by Reference — 4m)

### Part (a) — Storage Classes in C

- **Role:** A storage class determines a variable's **storage location**, **default initial value**, **visibility (scope)**, and **lifetime**:

| Storage Class | Storage Location | Default Initial Value | Scope | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `auto` | Stack (RAM) | Garbage (indeterminate) | Local to block | Until enclosing block exits |
| `register` | CPU register (or stack) | Garbage (indeterminate) | Local to block | Until enclosing block exits (`&` address-of illegal) |
| `static` | Data/BSS segment | `0` | Block (local) or file (internal linkage) | Entire program execution |
| `extern` | Data/BSS segment | `0` | Global across translation units | Entire program execution |

```c
#include <stdio.h>
extern int shared_cfg;          /* declared here; defined in another file */
void counter(void) {
    auto int local = 1;         /* recreated every call */
    static int calls = 0;       /* persists across calls */
    printf("local=%d, calls=%d\n", local, ++calls);
}
```

### Part (b) — Call by Value vs Call by Reference

> [!COMPARE] Call by Value vs Call by Reference in C
> | Parameter | Call by Value | Call by Reference (Address Passing) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **What Is Passed** | Copies of actual argument **values** (`swap(x, y)`). | Memory **addresses** (pointers) of actual variables (`swap(&x, &y)`). |
> | **Caller Modification** | Changes to formal parameters **do not** affect caller variables. | Dereferencing (`*p`) modifies the caller's original variables directly. |
> | **Memory Overhead** | Separate local copy created for each argument. | Copies only fixed-size pointer addresses (`4` or `8` bytes). |
> | **Multiple Outputs** | Can return at most one scalar value via `return`. | Can update multiple caller variables simultaneously. |

```c
void by_val(int x)  { x = 99; }       /* caller variable unchanged */
void by_ref(int *p) { *p = 99; }      /* caller variable becomes 99 */
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 6 Marks: Definition & Type System (1 Mark) + Core Built-In Data Types & Verified Examples (5 Marks)

### 1. Concept of Data Types in Python (1 Mark)

In Python, **every value is a heap-allocated object** whose **data type (class)** governs its memory representation, mutability, and valid operations. Variables are untyped references checked dynamically at runtime via `type(obj)`.

### 2. Core Built-In Data Types (5 Marks)

| Category | Built-In Type(s) | Mutability | Literal Example & Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Numeric** | `int`, `float`, `complex` | Immutable | `25`, `9.81`, `3 + 4j` — arbitrary-precision integers, IEEE-754 floats, complex numbers. |
| **Boolean** | `bool` (subclass of `int`) | Immutable | `True` (`1`), `False` (`0`) — logical truth outcomes. |
| **Text Sequence** | `str` | Immutable | `'Diploma CST'` — ordered Unicode character sequence supporting indexing/slicing. |
| **Sequence Containers** | `list`, `tuple`, `range` | `list` mutable; `tuple`/`range` immutable | `[10, 20]`, `(10, 20)`, `range(1, 5)` — ordered positional collections. |
| **Mapping** | `dict` | Mutable | `{'roll': 101, 'dept': 'CST'}` — `O(1)` hash-table key-value lookup. |
| **Set Types** | `set`, `frozenset` | `set` mutable; `frozenset` immutable | `{1, 2, 3}` — unordered unique hashable items supporting `|`, `&`, `-`. |
| **Null Singleton** | `NoneType` | Immutable | `None` — represents the absence of a value. |

```python
samples = [42, 3.14, 2 + 5j, True, "Python", [1, 2], (3, 4), {"k": 9}, {7, 7, 8}, None]
for item in samples:
    print(f"{repr(item):12} -> {type(item).__name__}")
```

- **Type Inspection & Casting:** Use `isinstance(x, int)` to test type membership safely and explicit constructors (`int()`, `float()`, `str()`, `list()`) for explicit conversion.

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 6 Marks: `list` vs `tuple` Comparison (3 Marks) + Key Features of Python (3 Marks)

### 1. Difference Between `list` and `tuple` in Python (3 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Python `list` vs `tuple`
> | Parameter | `list` | `tuple` |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Mutability** | **Mutable** — items can be reassigned, appended, popped, or sorted in place. | **Immutable** — fixed once constructed (`TypeError` on item assignment). |
> | **Literal Syntax** | Square brackets: `[10, 20, 30]`. | Parentheses + commas: `(10, 20, 30)` (singleton `(10,)`). |
> | **Methods & Hashability** | `11` methods; **unhashable** (cannot be a `dict` key or `set` item). | Only `.count()` & `.index()`; **hashable** if all items are hashable. |
> | **Memory & Speed** | Over-allocates pointer slots for dynamic growth. | Compact fixed block; faster construction and iteration. |

```python
lst = [1, 2, 3]; lst[0] = 99      # Valid -> [99, 2, 3]
tpl = (1, 2, 3)                   # tpl[0] = 99 raises TypeError
```

### 2. Key Features of Python (3 Marks)

- **Readable Indentation-Driven Syntax:** Clean English-like statements eliminate semicolon and brace clutter.
- **Interpreted & Cross-Platform:** Portable bytecode runs unchanged on Linux, Windows, macOS, and Termux.
- **Dynamically & Strongly Typed:** Runtime object binding without unsafe implicit string/number coercion.
- **Multi-Paradigm:** Supports procedural, object-oriented (`class`), and functional (`lambda`, comprehensions) styles.
- **Automatic Garbage Collection:** Reference counting plus cyclic garbage collector manages heap memory automatically.
- **"Batteries-Included" Library Ecosystem:** Rich standard library (`os`, `json`, `datetime`, `sqlite3`) plus PyPI packages (`NumPy`, `Pandas`, `Django`).

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 6 Marks: Mathematical Rule & Edge Cases (1 Mark) + Verified Python Program (3 Marks) + Dry-Run Trace & Output (2 Marks)

### 1. Mathematical Definition (1 Mark)

> [!FORMULA] Factorial Recurrence & Base Cases
> For any non-negative integer `n >= 0`: `0! = 1`, `1! = 1`, and `n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × ... × n` for `n >= 2`. Factorial is undefined for negative integers.

### 2. Python Program (Iterative `O(n)` Time, `O(1)` Space) (3 Marks)

```python
def factorial_of(n: int) -> int:
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Factorial is not defined for negative integers.")
    fact = 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        fact *= i
    return fact


for num in [0, 5, 7]:
    print(f"{num}! = {factorial_of(num)}")
```

### 3. Dry-Run Trace (`n = 5`) & Verified Output (2 Marks)

| Pass (`i`) | Operation (`fact = fact * i`) | Updated `fact` |
|---|---|---|
| Init | `fact = 1` | `1` |
| `i = 2` | `1 * 2` | `2` |
| `i = 3` | `2 * 3` | `6` |
| `i = 4` | `6 * 4` | `24` |
| `i = 5` | `24 * 5` | `120` |

```text
0! = 1
5! = 120
7! = 5040
```

- **Why Iterative Beats Naive Recursion:** Avoids CPython's `RecursionError` call-stack limit (`~1000` frames) while `O(1)` auxiliary space and Python's arbitrary-precision `int` compute huge factorials (`100!`) without 64-bit integer overflow.
- **Standard-Library Shortcut:** `math.factorial(n)` from `import math` implements the same non-negative factorial check in optimized C.

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 6 Marks: `for` Loop (2 Marks) + `while` Loop (2 Marks) + Nested Loops & Loop-Control Clauses (2 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Python `for` Loop vs `while` Loop
> | Parameter | `for` Loop (Definite / Iterator-Driven) | `while` Loop (Indefinite / Condition-Driven) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Driving Mechanism** | Pulls items automatically from any iterable (`range`, `list`, `str`, `dict`). | Re-evaluates a Boolean condition before every pass. |
> | **Counter Update** | Automatic via the iterator protocol (`__next__()`). | Programmer must update loop state manually to avoid infinite loops. |

### 1. `for` Loop with Example (2 Marks)

```python
total = 0
for k in range(1, 6):       # Visits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
    total += k
print("Sum 1..5 =", total)  # Verified Output: Sum 1..5 = 15
```

### 2. `while` Loop with Example (2 Marks)

```python
n = 4
while n > 0:
    print(n, end=" ")
    n -= 1                  # State update toward termination
# Verified Output: 4 3 2 1
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 6 Marks: Palindrome Logic (1 Mark) + Arithmetic Digit-Reversal Program (3 Marks) + Dry-Run Trace & Slicing Alternative (2 Marks)

### 1. Concept of a Palindrome Number (1 Mark)

An integer is a **palindrome** if its decimal digits read identically forward and backward (for example, `1221`, `909`, `7`; negative integers like `-121` are not palindromes because of the leading `'-'` sign).

### 2. Python Program Using Arithmetic Digit Reversal (3 Marks)

```python
def is_palindrome_number(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 0:
        return False
    original = n
    reversed_num = 0
    while n > 0:
        digit = n % 10                       # Extract rightmost digit
        reversed_num = reversed_num * 10 + digit
        n //= 10                             # Drop rightmost digit
    return original == reversed_num


for candidate in [1221, 1234, 7, -121]:
    verdict = "Palindrome" if is_palindrome_number(candidate) else "Not Palindrome"
    print(f"{candidate:5d} -> {verdict}")
```

### 3. Dry-Run (`n = 121`) & Concise Slicing Check (2 Marks)

- **Trace on `121`:** Pass 1: `digit=1, rev=1, n=12` -> Pass 2: `digit=2, rev=12, n=1` -> Pass 3: `digit=1, rev=121, n=0` -> `original == rev` (`True`).
- **Complexity:** Runs in **`O(d)`** time (`d = floor(log10(n)) + 1` digits) and **`O(1)`** auxiliary space without allocating intermediate strings.
- **Pythonic String-Slice One-Liner:** `n >= 0 and str(n) == str(n)[::-1]`.

```text
 1221 -> Palindrome
 1234 -> Not Palindrome
    7 -> Palindrome
 -121 -> Not Palindrome
```

### 2. Using Input and Output Files Together in Python (4 Marks)

Using Python's `with open(...)` **context manager** guarantees both streams flush buffers and close automatically even if an exception occurs:

```python
# Step 1: Create sample input file
with open("marks_in.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as seed:
    seed.write("Riya,88\nArjun,76\nNeha,92\n")
```

```python
def manual_length(text: str) -> int:

for sample in ["Diploma CST", "", "Python 3.12!"]:
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (a) 5 Marks + (b) 3 Marks

### (a) Definition & Key Features of Python Programming (5 Marks)

**Python** is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed, multi-paradigm general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum (first released in 1991) that prioritizes clean readability through significant indentation.

- **Readable English-Like Syntax:** Eliminates curly braces and semicolons, reducing boilerplate lines by `3–5x` compared with C or Java.
- **Interpreted Bytecode Execution:** Compiles source code into portable `.pyc` bytecode executed by the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) with instant interactive REPL testing.
- **Dynamic & Strong Typing:** Variables bind to typed objects at runtime without type declarations while forbidding unsafe implicit string/number coercion.
- **Multi-Paradigm Support:** Combines procedural scripting, full Object-Oriented Programming (`class`, inheritance, dunder protocols), and functional tools (`lambda`, comprehensions, generators).
- **Automatic Memory Management:** Reference counting paired with a cyclic generational garbage collector reclaims unused heap objects automatically.
- **"Batteries-Included" Standard Library & Ecosystem:** Ships rich built-in modules (`os`, `re`, `json`, `datetime`, `sqlite3`) plus PyPI packages (`NumPy`, `Pandas`, `Django`).
- **Cross-Platform Portability:** Runs unchanged across Linux, Windows, macOS, and Android/Termux.

### (b) Difference Between Local and Global Variables (3 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Local Variable vs Global Variable in Python
> | Parameter | Local Variable | Global Variable |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Where Defined** | Assigned inside a `def` function body or parameter list. | Assigned at the top module level outside every function. |
> | **Visibility Scope** | Restricted strictly to that function call (`NameError` outside). | Readable across the entire module; rebound inside functions via `global`. |
> | **Lifetime** | Allocated on function entry; freed when the call frame returns. | Persists from module import/start until program exit. |

```python
rate = 10                   # Global variable
def compute(principal):
    interest = principal * rate / 100   # 'interest' is local; 'rate' read from global
    return interest

print(compute(2500))        # Verified Output: 250.0
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (a) 3 Marks + (b) 2 Marks + (c) 3 Marks

### (a) `join()` and `split()` String Methods with Examples (3 Marks)

- **`str.split(sep=None, maxsplit=-1)`:** Breaks a string into a **`list[str]`** around `sep` (when `sep` is omitted, splits on arbitrary whitespace runs and strips leading/trailing whitespace).
- **`sep.join(iterable)`:** Inverse operation — concatenates an iterable of strings into **one `str`** in `O(n)` time, inserting `sep` strictly between adjacent items.

```python
line = "apple,banana,mango"
tokens = line.split(",")         # ['apple', 'banana', 'mango']
rejoined = " | ".join(tokens)    # 'apple | banana | mango'
print(tokens, "->", rejoined)
```

### (b) Mutable vs Immutable Data Types in Python (2 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Mutable vs Immutable Data Types
> | Parameter | Mutable Data Types | Immutable Data Types |
> |---|---|---|
> | **In-Place Change** | State/elements can be altered after creation while keeping `id(obj)` unchanged. | State cannot be altered once created; transformations return a new object. |
> | **Built-In Examples** | `list`, `dict`, `set`, `bytearray` | `int`, `float`, `complex`, `bool`, `str`, `tuple`, `frozenset`, `bytes` |

### (c) Why Strings Are Immutable in Python (with Example) (3 Marks)

- **Hashability for Dictionary Keys & Sets:** Keeping a string's character buffer fixed guarantees its `hash(s)` value never changes, allowing `O(1)` lookup as `dict` keys and `set` members.
- **String Interning & Memory Sharing:** CPython safely shares identical identifier/short string objects in memory without defensive copying.
- **Safety Against Alien Mutation:** Passing a filename or URL string into a helper function can never corrupt the caller's string.

```python
s = "cat"
before_id = id(s)
# s[0] = 'b'                     # Raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
s = "b" + s[1:]                  # Creates a brand-new string object 'bat'
print(s, id(s) != before_id)     # Verified Output: bat True
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (a) 4 Marks + (b) 4 Marks

### (a) `break` and `continue` Statements in a `for` Loop (4 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] `break` vs `continue` in Python `for` Loops
> | Parameter | `break` Statement | `continue` Statement |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Control Transfer** | Exits the innermost enclosing loop **completely** and jumps past the loop suite. | Skips the rest of the **current pass** and advances to the next item from the iterator. |
> | **Remaining Elements** | Never inspected. | Processed normally on subsequent iterations. |
> | **Loop `else:` Interaction** | Suppresses execution of any attached `for ... else:` block. | Allows `for ... else:` to run normally once all items finish. |

```python
for i in range(1, 8):
    if i == 3:
        continue          # Skip 3 only
    if i == 6:
        break             # Stop completely when i reaches 6
    print(i, end=" ")     # Verified Output: 1 2 4 5 
```

### (b) Python Program to Check Whether a Number Is Prime (4 Marks)

```python
def check_prime(n: int) -> str:
    if n < 2:
        return f"{n} is NOT Prime (primes are integers >= 2)"
    for divisor in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if n % divisor == 0:
            return f"{n} is NOT Prime (divisible by {divisor})"
    return f"{n} is Prime"


for candidate in [1, 2, 19, 25]:
    print(check_prime(candidate))
```

- **Verified Output:**

```text
1 is NOT Prime (primes are integers >= 2)
2 is Prime
19 is Prime
25 is NOT Prime (divisible by 5)
```

- **Efficiency (`O(√n)`):** Any composite `n = a × b` has at least one factor `<= √n`, so testing `range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)` avoids redundant upper-half checks.

### (a) Dictionary & Its Built-In Methods (4 Marks)

A **dictionary (`dict`)** is a mutable, insertion-ordered hash-table mapping **unique, immutable/hashable keys** to arbitrary value objects in `O(1)` average lookup time.

| Method | Behaviour & Example |
|---|---|
| `d.get(k, default=None)` | Safely returns value for `k`, or `default` instead of raising `KeyError`. |
| `d.keys()` / `d.values()` / `d.items()` | Dynamic view objects of keys, values, and `(key, value)` pairs. |
| `d.update(other)` | Inserts/overwrites multiple key-value pairs from another mapping or pairs. |
| `d.pop(k[, default])` | Removes key `k` and returns its associated value. |
| `d.popitem()` | Removes and returns the **last-inserted** `(key, value)` tuple (LIFO). |
| `d.setdefault(k, val)` | Returns `d[k]` if present; otherwise inserts `d[k] = val` and returns `val`. |
| `d.clear()` / `d.copy()` | Empties dictionary in place / creates a shallow copy. |

```python
student = {"roll": 101, "name": "Riya"}
student.update({"dept": "CST", "cgpa": 8.9})
print(student.get("dept"), student.pop("roll"), list(student.keys()))
# Output: CST 101 ['name', 'dept', 'cgpa']
```

### (b) Differentiate Between Tuple and List in Python (4 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Python `tuple` vs `list`
> | Parameter | `tuple` | `list` |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Mutability** | **Immutable** — elements cannot be reassigned, added, or removed. | **Mutable** — supports item assignment, `.append()`, `.extend()`, `.pop()`, `.sort()`. |
> | **Literal Syntax** | Parentheses + commas: `(10, 20, 30)` (singleton `(10,)`). | Square brackets: `[10, 20, 30]`. |
> | **Built-In Methods** | Only `2` non-mutating methods: `.count()` and `.index()`. | `11` methods including in-place mutators. |
> | **Hashability & Dict Keys** | Hashable when all items are hashable (`valid dict key`). | Unhashable (`TypeError` as a `dict` key or `set` element). |
> | **Memory & Performance** | Single compact allocation; faster literal creation and iteration. | Over-allocated dynamic pointer array to amortize `.append()` growth. |

### (a) Purpose of the `return` Statement in Python Functions (4 Marks)

- **Immediate Frame Exit:** Executing `return expr` immediately terminates the active function call (any lines written after `return` in the same block are unreachable) and pops its stack frame.
- **Value Handback & Multi-Value Tuple Packing:** Sends the evaluated object back to the caller expression; comma-separated expressions (`return q, r`) pack a **`tuple`** cleanly, while a bare `return` (or reaching the end of the function with no `return`) implicitly returns `None`.

```python
def div_and_rem(a: int, b: int):
    return a // b, a % b      # Packs and returns a 2-tuple

q, r = div_and_rem(17, 5)
print(f"Quotient={q}, Remainder={r}")   # Verified Output: Quotient=3, Remainder=2
```

### (b) Required Arguments vs Default Arguments (4 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Required Arguments vs Default Arguments
> | Parameter | Required Arguments | Default Arguments |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Header Syntax** | Declared without `=` fallback (`def area(l, w):`). | Declared with `=` fallback (`def power(x, exp=2):`). |
> | **Call-Site Obligation** | **Mandatory** — omitting one raises `TypeError: missing required positional argument`. | **Optional** — omitted argument uses the header fallback; passing a value overrides it. |
> | **Parameter-Order Rule** | Must appear **before** any default parameters in `def`. | Must appear **after** all required positional parameters. |

```python
def enroll(name, semester=3):     # 'name' is required; 'semester' has default 3
    return f"{name} -> Sem {semester}"

print(enroll("Arjun"))            # Uses default -> Arjun -> Sem 3
print(enroll("Arjun", 5))         # Overrides default -> Arjun -> Sem 5
```

- **Important Rule:** Default values are evaluated **once** when `def` executes, so immutable defaults (`int`, `str`, `None`) should always be preferred over mutable `[]` or `{}` defaults.

### (a) Seven Operator Families in Python with Examples (4 Marks)

| Operator Family | Symbols | Verified Example & Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Arithmetic** | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `//`, `%`, `**` | `17 // 5 -> 3`, `17 % 5 -> 2`, `2 ** 4 -> 16` |
| **Relational (Comparison)** | `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` | `10 >= 8 -> True` (supports chaining: `1 < x < 10`) |
| **Logical (Boolean)** | `and`, `or`, `not` | `True and False -> False`, `not 0 -> True` |
| **Assignment (Augmented)** | `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `//=`, `%=`, `**=`, `:=` | `x = 10; x += 5 -> x == 15` |
| **Bitwise** | `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` | `5 & 3 -> 1`, `5 | 3 -> 7`, `~5 -> -6`, `5 << 1 -> 10` |
| **Membership** | `in`, `not in` | `'py' in 'python' -> True`, `9 not in [1, 2] -> True` |
| **Identity** | `is`, `is not` | `x is None -> True` (compares memory address `id(a) == id(b)`) |

### (b) Importing a Module in Python — Four Idiomatic Forms (4 Marks)

A module is loaded once per session from `sys.path` into `sys.modules` using the `import` statement:

- **Full Module Import (`import mod`):** Keeps the module's namespace intact so names never collide (`math.sqrt(25)`).
- **Aliased Import (`import mod as alias`):** Binds a concise nickname for frequently used libraries (`import math as m`, `import numpy as np`).
- **Selective Attribute Import (`from mod import name1, name2`):** Imports only specific functions or constants directly into the current local namespace.
- **Package Submodule Import (`from pkg import submod`):** Loads a specific module housed inside a multi-module package directory while avoiding star-import (`from mod import *`) namespace pollution.

```python
import math
import random as rnd
from math import factorial, pi

print(math.sqrt(49))               # 7.0
print(factorial(5), round(pi, 4))  # 120 3.1416
print(1 <= rnd.randint(1, 6) <= 6) # True
```

### (a) Module and Package in Python (2 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Python Module vs Python Package
> | Parameter | Module | Package |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Definition** | A **single `.py` file** grouping reusable functions, classes, and constants (`math.py`). | A **directory** containing multiple `.py` modules (traditionally with `__init__.py`). |

### (b) Arbitrary Arguments (`*args` and `**kwargs`) with Example (3 Marks)

When the exact number of arguments is unknown at definition time, Python provides two variadic parameter forms:
- **`*args` (Arbitrary Positional):** Packs all surplus positional arguments into a **`tuple`**.
- **`**kwargs` (Arbitrary Keyword):** Packs all surplus `name=value` keyword arguments into a **`dict`**.

```python
def summarize_order(customer, *items, **options):
    print("Customer:", customer)
    print("Items tuple:", items)
    print("Options dict:", options)

summarize_order("Riya", "Book", "Pen", express=True, discount=10)
# Output:
# Customer: Riya
# Items tuple: ('Book', 'Pen')
# Options dict: {'express': True, 'discount': 10}
```

### (c) Python Code to Print Current Date and Time (3 Marks)

```python
from datetime import datetime

now = datetime.now()   # Fetches current local system date & time
print("ISO Timestamp :", now)
print("Formatted     :", now.strftime("%d-%m-%Y %H:%M:%S"))
```

- **Sample Output:**

```text
ISO Timestamp : 2026-11-26 14:35:10.482910
Formatted     : 26-11-2026 14:35:10
```

- **Explanation:** `datetime.now()` queries the system clock and returns a `datetime` instance exposing `.year`, `.month`, `.day`, `.hour`, `.minute`, and `.second` integer attributes, while `.strftime()` formats those fields into any custom human-readable timestamp pattern (`%d` zero-padded day, `%m` month, `%Y` 4-digit year, and `%H:%M:%S` 24-hour clock).

### (a) File Access Modes in Python with Examples (4 Marks)

| Mode | Stream Offset | Behaviour on Existing / Missing File |
|---|---|---|
| `'r'` | `0` (start) | Read-only text (default); raises `FileNotFoundError` if missing. |
| `'w'` | `0` (start) | Write-only text; creates missing file or **truncates** existing file to `0` bytes. |
| `'a'` | `EOF` (end) | Append-only text; creates missing file and writes strictly at the end. |
| `'x'` | `0` (start) | Exclusive creation; fails with `FileExistsError` if file already exists. |
| `'r+'` / `'w+'` / `'a+'` | `0` / `0` / `EOF` | Combined read + write (`'w+'` truncates; `'r+'` preserves; `'a+'` appends). |
| `'rb'` / `'wb'` | `0` (start) | Binary mode — transfers raw `bytes` without newline translation or UTF-8 decoding. |

```python
with open("report.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Appended summary line\n")
```

### (b) File Object Methods: `(i) read()` and `(ii) write()` (4 Marks)

- **`(i) f.read(size=-1)`:** Reads at most `size` characters in text mode (or `size` bytes in binary mode) from the current file pointer and advances the pointer; when `size` is omitted or negative, reads until `EOF` and returns `''` on subsequent calls at `EOF`.
- **`(ii) f.write(data)`:** Writes string `data` (or `bytes` in `'wb'` mode) at the current stream position **without** automatically appending `'\n'`, returning the integer count of characters/bytes written.

```python
with open("demo.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    written = out.write("Hello Python!\nSecond line")

with open("demo.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as inp:
    head = inp.read(5)      # Reads first 5 chars -> 'Hello'
    rest = inp.read()       # Reads remainder from offset 5 to EOF
print(written, repr(head), repr(rest))
# Output: 25 'Hello' ' Python!\nSecond line'
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (a) 3 Marks + (b) 5 Marks

### (a) MVC Framework — Each Component Explained (3 Marks)

**MVC (Model–View–Controller)** structures web applications into three decoupled layers so database schemas, business rules, and UI templates evolve independently:

- **Model (`1m`):** Represents persistent application data, validation rules, and ORM database tables (`models.py`).
- **View (`1m`):** Renders domain data into user-facing presentation markup such as HTML or JSON.
- **Controller (`1m`):** Intercepts HTTP requests, coordinates Model queries/updates, and dispatches data to the appropriate View (in Django's **MVT** terminology, `urls.py` + `views.py` perform Controller duties and `templates/` render HTML).

### (b) Step-by-Step Guide to Creating & Running a Django Project (5 Marks)

1. **Create & Activate an Isolated Virtual Environment:** Prevents global package version conflicts.
2. **Install Django via `pip`:** Downloads the latest stable Django release.
3. **Scaffold Project & App (`startproject` / `startapp`):** Generates `manage.py`, `settings.py`, `urls.py`, and WSGI/ASGI entrypoints.
4. **Apply Initial Database Migrations (`migrate`):** Initializes built-in auth, session, and admin tables in `db.sqlite3`.
5. **Launch Development Server (`runserver`):** Starts the local HTTP server on `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`.

```bash
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate              # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install django
django-admin startproject college_hub
cd college_hub
python manage.py startapp students    # Optional modular app inside project
python manage.py migrate              # Create initial SQLite tables
python manage.py runserver            # Serves at http://127.0.0.1:8000/
```

- **Project Layout Created:** `manage.py` (command-line utility for migrations, superuser creation, and running the server) + `college_hub/{__init__.py, settings.py, urls.py, wsgi.py, asgi.py}`.

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (i) 2 Marks + (ii) 3 Marks + (iii) 3 Marks

### (i) Purpose of Indentation in Python (2 Marks)

- **Lexical Block Grouping:** Python replaces C/Java curly braces `{ ... }` with consistent leading whitespace (**4 spaces per level** under PEP 8) to delimit compound suites (`if`, `for`, `while`, `def`, `class`, `try`).
- **Syntax & Logic Safety:** Increasing indentation opens a nested suite, dedenting closes it, and inconsistent indentation triggers `IndentationError` at compile time.

### (ii) Difference Between a `list` and a `tuple` (3 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Python `list` vs `tuple`
> | Parameter | `list` | `tuple` |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Mutability** | **Mutable** — supports item assignment, `.append()`, `.pop()`, `.sort()`. | **Immutable** — size and element bindings are fixed (`TypeError` on assignment). |
> | **Literal Syntax** | Square brackets: `[10, 20, 30]`. | Parentheses / trailing comma: `(10, 20, 30)` or `(10,)`. |
> | **Memory & Speed** | Over-allocates growth buffer (slightly larger memory footprint). | Compact single fixed block; faster construction and iteration. |
> | **Dictionary Key / Set Use** | Unhashable — **cannot** be used as a `dict` key. | Hashable (when elements are immutable) — valid as `dict` keys. |

```python
scores = [75, 80, 90]
scores[0] = 78                 # Valid in-place mutation
point = (22.57, 88.36)         # Immutable coordinate tuple
```

### (iii) `if` Statement & Decision Making in Code (3 Marks)

- **Decision Mechanism:** An `if ... elif ... else:` ladder evaluates Boolean expressions top-to-bottom and executes **only the first suite** whose condition evaluates to truthy, falling back to `else:` when all conditions are falsy:

```python
marks = 74
if marks >= 80:
    grade = "Distinction"
elif marks >= 60:
    grade = "First Class"
elif marks >= 40:
    grade = "Pass"
else:
    grade = "Fail"
print(f"Marks={marks} -> {grade}")   # Verified Output: Marks=74 -> First Class
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (i) 4 Marks + (ii) 4 Marks

### (i) List Slicing Explained with Examples (4 Marks)

- **Syntax & Half-Open Rule:** `lst[start:stop:step]` extracts a **new shallow-copied `list`** starting at index `start` (inclusive, default `0`), stopping strictly before `stop` (exclusive, default `len(lst)`), and advancing by non-zero stride `step` (default `1`).
- **Graceful Boundary Clamping & Negative Stride:** Out-of-range slice endpoints clamp silently without raising `IndexError` (`a[2:99]` safely stops at the end), slice assignment (`a[1:3] = [99]`) replaces sub-ranges in place on mutable lists, and negative `step` (`-1`) traverses right-to-left:

```python
a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
print(a[1:4])      # [20, 30, 40]        (indices 1, 2, 3)
print(a[:3])       # [10, 20, 30]        (start defaults to 0)
print(a[::2])      # [10, 30, 50]        (every 2nd element)
print(a[::-1])     # [60, 50, 40, 30, 20, 10] (full reversed copy)
```

### (ii) Python Dictionary Explained with Example (4 Marks)

- **Definition:** A Python `dict` is a **mutable, insertion-ordered associative hash table** (guaranteed insertion order since Python 3.7) storing `key: value` pairs enclosed in `{...}`.
- **Key & Value Rules:** Keys must be **unique and hashable** (`str`, `int`, `tuple` of immutables) providing `O(1)` average lookup, insertion, and deletion; values may be arbitrary objects.
- **Core Operations:** Read via `d[key]` or safe `d.get(key, default)`, update via `d[key] = val`, remove via `d.pop(key)`, and iterate via `d.items()`:

```python
student = {"roll": 101, "name": "Riya", "marks": 85}
student["city"] = "Kolkata"                   # Insert new key-value pair
student["marks"] = 89                         # Update existing key
print(student["name"], student.get("dept", "CST"))  # Riya CST
for k, v in student.items():
    print(f"{k}={v}", end=" ")                # roll=101 name=Riya marks=89 city=Kolkata 
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (i) 3 Marks + (ii) 5 Marks

### (i) How a `for` Loop Differs from a `while` Loop (3 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] `for` Loop vs `while` Loop in Python
> | Parameter | `for` Loop (Definite Iteration) | `while` Loop (Indefinite Iteration) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Control Mechanism** | Pulls items automatically from any iterable (`list`, `str`, `range`, `file`) via `iter()`/`next()`. | Re-evaluates a Boolean condition before every pass until it becomes falsy. |
> | **State / Update Management** | Progression is automatic — no manual counter increment needed. | Programmer must explicitly update state inside the body or risk an infinite loop. |
> | **Primary Use Case** | Known element count or direct collection traversal. | Convergence checks, sentinel input loops, and digit-extraction loops (`while n > 0`). |

### (ii) Python Program to Compute Sum of Digits of a Number (5 Marks)

```python
def sum_of_digits(n: int) -> int:
    num = abs(n)          # Handle negative integers cleanly (e.g., -409 -> 13)
    total = 0
    while num > 0:
        digit = num % 10  # Extract least-significant decimal digit
        total += digit
        num //= 10        # Strip least-significant digit via floor division
    return total


for sample in [4582, -307, 0]:
    print(f"sum_of_digits({sample}) = {sum_of_digits(sample)}")
```

- **Step-by-Step Dry-Run Trace (`n = 4582`):**

| Pass | `num` (Entry) | `digit = num % 10` | `total` (Updated) | `num //= 10` (Exit) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `1` | `4582` | `2` | `0 + 2 = 2` | `458` |
| `2` | `458` | `8` | `2 + 8 = 10` | `45` |
| `3` | `45` | `5` | `10 + 5 = 15` | `4` |
| `4` | `4` | `4` | `15 + 4 = 19` | `0` (loop terminates) |

- **Complexity:** `O(d)` time (where `d = ⌊log₁₀(|n|)⌋ + 1` digits) and `O(1)` auxiliary space.

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (i) 3 Marks + (ii) 2 Marks + (iii) 3 Marks

### (i) Positional Arguments (3 Marks)

- **Mechanism:** Positional arguments are bound to formal function parameters strictly **by left-to-right position** (`1st` argument → `1st` parameter, `2nd` argument → `2nd` parameter).
- **Strict Arity & Order:** Passing too few or too many positional arguments raises `TypeError`, and swapping argument order changes the computed result:

```python
def power_diff(base, exp):
    return base ** exp

print(power_diff(2, 5))   # base=2, exp=5 -> 32
print(power_diff(5, 2))   # base=5, exp=2 -> 25  (order changes result)
```

### (ii) Default Arguments (2 Marks)

- **Mechanism:** Assigning a fallback value (`tax=0.18`) in the `def` signature makes that parameter optional when omitted by the caller; in Python's grammar, every required non-default parameter must strictly precede any parameter with a default value (`SyntaxError` otherwise).

```python
def bill(amount, tax=0.18):
    return round(amount * (1 + tax), 2)

print(bill(1000), bill(1000, 0.05))   # Output: 1180.0 1050.0
```

> [!TRAP] Mutable Default Argument Pitfall
> Default expressions are evaluated **once at `def` definition time**, so use `items=None` instead of mutable `items=[]`.

### (iii) Variable-Length Arguments (`*args` and `**kwargs`) (3 Marks)

- **`*args` (Non-Keyword Variadic Tuple):** Collects any number of extra positional arguments into an immutable **`tuple`**.
- **`**kwargs` (Keyword Variadic Dictionary):** Collects any number of extra `key=value` keyword arguments into a **`dict`**.

```python
def report(title, *scores, **details):
    avg = sum(scores) / len(scores) if scores else 0.0
    return f"{title}: avg={avg:.1f}, info={details}"

print(report("Sem-3", 80, 85, 90, dept="CST", batch=2026))
# Verified Output: Sem-3: avg=85.0, info={'dept': 'CST', 'batch': 2026}
```

### (i) File Opening Modes in Python with Examples (6 Marks)

`open(file, mode='r', encoding=...)` combines an **access mode** (`r`, `w`, `a`, `x`, `+`) with a **data format flag** (`t` text default, `b` raw bytes):

| Mode | File Pointer Start | If File Missing | If File Exists | Primary Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `'r'` | Beginning (`0`) | Raises `FileNotFoundError` | Preserves content | Read-only text (default mode). |
| `'w'` | Beginning (`0`) | Creates new file | **Truncates** to `0` bytes | Overwrite/create fresh output file. |
| `'a'` | End of file (`EOF`) | Creates new file | Preserves; writes at end | Append audit/event logs safely. |
| `'x'` | Beginning (`0`) | Creates new file | Raises `FileExistsError` | Atomic exclusive file creation. |
| `'r+'` | Beginning (`0`) | Raises `FileNotFoundError` | Preserves content | Read + write without initial truncation. |
| `'w+'` | Beginning (`0`) | Creates new file | **Truncates** to `0` bytes | Write + read scratch file. |
| `'a+'` | End of file (`EOF`) | Creates new file | Appends at EOF + allows read | Append + read (seek to read earlier data). |
| `'rb'` / `'wb'` | `0` | Same as `'r'` / `'w'` | Raw `bytes` (no UTF-8/CRLF decoding) | Images, PDFs, ZIPs, `pickle` binary streams. |

```python
with open("audit.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as log:
    log.write("2026-01-15: Login OK\n")

with open("logo.png", "rb") as img:
    magic_header = img.read(8)        # Returns raw bytes object
```

- **Regex Text Pattern Matching:** Inspecting strings against declarative **regular expression** grammars (`import re`) to validate formats (emails, PIN codes), extract tokens (`re.findall(r"\d+", s)`), or substitute text (`re.sub()`).
- **Structural Pattern Matching (Python 3.10+):** Matching data shapes, sequences, and mappings declaratively via `match subject: case pattern:` blocks.

### (i) What Is MVC? (3 Marks)

**MVC (Model–View–Controller)** is a three-tier software design pattern that decouples data persistence, user interface presentation, and request-routing logic:

- **Model:** Manages domain state, validation rules, and database queries.
- **View:** Formats Model data into the visual presentation (HTML/JSON) seen by the user.
- **Controller:** Accepts incoming user input/HTTP requests, invokes Model operations, and chooses which View renders the response (in Django, this maps to **MVT — Model–View–Template**, where Django's URL dispatcher + View act as Controller and the Template renders HTML).

```ascii
Client Browser ---> [ Controller (URLs/View) ] <---> [ Model (ORM / DB) ]
         ^                      |
         +--- HTML Response ----+---> [ View / Template ]
```

### (ii) What Is Django and Why You Should Use It (5 Marks)

- **Definition:** **Django** is a free, open-source, high-level **"batteries-included" Python web framework** engineered for rapid, clean, pragmatic development of database-driven web applications.
- **Five Key Reasons to Use Django:**
  1. **Built-In Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) & Migrations:** Define tables as Python classes (`models.Model`) and switch between SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL without rewriting SQL.
  2. **Automatic Admin Interface:** Generates a production-ready CRUD back-office dashboard directly from registered models.
  3. **Enterprise Security Defaults:** Protects automatically against SQL injection, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Cross-Site Request Forgery (`{% csrf_token %}`), and clickjacking.
  4. **Authentication, Forms & Sessions Included:** Ships complete user login, permissions, password hashing, and form validation out of the box.
  5. **Scalability &DRY Ecosystem:** Clean app modularity (`startapp`), caching hooks, and packages like Django REST Framework (`DRF`).

```bash
pip install django
django-admin startproject portal
cd portal && python manage.py migrate && python manage.py runserver
```

### (i) Program to Print Elements of a Tuple Using a `for` Loop (4 Marks)

```python
subjects = ("C Programming", "Python", "Data Structures", "CSO", "Algorithms")

print("Index | Subject Name")
print("------+------------------")
for idx, name in enumerate(subjects, start=1):
    print(f"  {idx}   | {name}")
```

- **Verified Output:**

```text
Index | Subject Name
------+------------------
  1   | C Programming
  2   | Python
  3   | Data Structures
  4   | CSO
  5   | Algorithms
```

- **Explanation:** `for` iterates directly over the immutable `tuple` (`enumerate()` pairs each item with its 1-based serial number cleanly without manual `range(len(...))` indexing, and tuple unpacking binds `(idx, name)` on every pass in `O(1)` extra space).

### (ii) Utility of the `pass` Statement (2 Marks)

- **Syntactic Null Operation:** Because Python's indentation grammar forbids empty indented suites, `pass` serves as a valid no-op statement placeholder during top-down design (stubbing unfinished functions, abstract classes, empty loops, or intentionally ignored `except` branches) without raising `IndentationError`:

```python
class PaymentGatewayError(Exception):
    pass   # Valid minimal custom exception class
```

### (iii) Utility of the `else` Clause of a `for` Loop (2 Marks)

- **No-`break` Completion Clause:** A `for ... else:` block runs **if and only if** the loop exhausts its iterable normally **without encountering a `break` statement** — eliminating manual Boolean `found = False` flag variables in search algorithms:

```python
nums = [12, 18, 25, 31]
for x in nums:
    if x % 7 == 0:
        print("Divisible by 7:", x)
        break
else:
    print("No multiple of 7 found")   # Runs because break never executed
```

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (i) 4 Marks + (ii) 4 Marks

### (i) Local vs Global Variables with Examples (4 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Local Variable vs Global Variable in Python
> | Parameter | Local Variable | Global Variable |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Declaration Place** | Assigned inside a `def` function body (or parameter list). | Assigned at the top module level outside all functions. |
> | **Visibility Scope** | Accessible **only inside** that function call (`NameError` outside). | Readable across all functions inside the same module. |
> | **Lifetime** | Created when the function is called; garbage-collected on `return`. | Exists from module load until program termination. |
> | **Rebinding Keyword** | Default for any `=` assignment inside a function. | Requires explicit `global var_name` inside a function to rebind. |

```python
counter = 100              # Global variable

def increment():
    global counter         # Declares intent to rebind module-level 'counter'
    step = 5               # Local variable (private to increment)
    counter += step
    print("Inside:", counter, step)

increment()                # Output: Inside: 105 5
print("Outside:", counter) # Output: Outside: 105
```

### (ii) Passing a List to a Function (Call-by-Object-Reference) (4 Marks)

In Python's **pass-by-object-reference** model, passing a `list` binds the formal parameter to the **same mutable list object** (`id(items) == id(scores)`), so in-place mutations (`append`, index assignment) are visible to the caller unless a copy (`scores[:]`) is passed:

```python
def curve_and_summarize(marks_list: list, bonus: int) -> dict:
    # In-place mutation updates the caller's list directly
    for i in range(len(marks_list)):
        marks_list[i] = min(100, marks_list[i] + bonus)
    return {
        "count": len(marks_list),
        "max": max(marks_list),
        "avg": round(sum(marks_list) / len(marks_list), 2),
    }


scores = [72, 85, 98]
summary = curve_and_summarize(scores, bonus=5)
print("Updated scores:", scores)     # Output: Updated scores: [77, 90, 100]
print("Summary:", summary)           # Output: Summary: {'count': 3, 'max': 100, 'avg': 89.0}
```

### (i) Basic Data Types Available in Python with Examples (5 Marks)

In Python, every value is a first-class heap object carrying a runtime type tag, reference count, and value. The core built-in data types are organized as follows:

| Category | Data Type | Mutable? | Example & Key Property |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Numeric** | `int`, `float`, `complex` | No | `age = 20`, `pi = 3.1415`, `z = 2 + 3j` (arbitrary-precision `int`, IEEE-754 `float`). |
| **Boolean** | `bool` | No | `is_valid = True` (`bool` subclasses `int`: `True == 1`, `False == 0`). |
| **Text Sequence** | `str` | No | `course = "Python"` (indexed Unicode character sequence). |
| **Ordered Sequences** | `list`, `tuple`, `range` | `list` only | `[75, 82, 90]`, `(4, 5)`, `range(1, 10, 2)`. |
| **Mapping** | `dict` | Yes | `{"roll": 101, "dept": "CST"}` (insertion-ordered hash table). |
| **Set Types** | `set`, `frozenset` | `set` only | `{10, 20, 30}` (unique hashable elements; fast `O(1)` membership). |
| **Null Singleton** | `NoneType` | No | `result = None` (represents absence of a return/assigned value). |

```python
student = {"roll": 12, "name": "Riya", "marks": [84, 91, 78], "passed": True}
print(type(student["roll"]).__name__, type(student["marks"]).__name__)   # int list
```

### (ii) Interpreter Type Conversion & Its Justification (3 Marks)

1. **Implicit Type Conversion (Numeric Coercion by Interpreter):** When an arithmetic expression mixes compatible numeric types, Python automatically widens the narrower operand along the **numeric tower** `bool -> int -> float -> complex`:
   - `5 + 2.5 -> 7.5` (`int` promoted to `float`); `True + 4 -> 5` (`bool` treated as `1`); `3 + 2j + 1.5 -> (4.5+2j)`.
2. **No Implicit Cross-Domain Coercion (Strong Typing):** Unlike JavaScript or PHP, Python **refuses** to coerce strings and numbers implicitly (`"25" + 5` raises `TypeError`), requiring **explicit constructor conversion** (`int("25") + 5 == 30`, `str(100)`, `float("3.5")`).
- **Justification:** Widening along `bool -> int -> float -> complex` is **lossless in magnitude/representation** (preventing silent truncation of fractional or imaginary parts), whereas rejecting implicit `str <-> int` coercion prevents silent data-corruption bugs when `'25' + 5` could mean either `30` or `'255'`.

> [!MARKS] Mark Distribution — Total 8 Marks: (i) 3 Marks + (ii) 2 Marks + (iii) 3 Marks

### (i) Working of `continue`, `break`, and `pass` in Loops (3 Marks)

- **`continue`:** Immediately skips the remaining statements of the **current** loop iteration and advances control to the next iteration header.
- **`break`:** Immediately terminates the **entire** innermost enclosing `for`/`while` loop (bypassing any loop `else:` block) and resumes after the loop.
- **`pass`:** A syntactic **no-op placeholder** that executes nothing at runtime, used where Python's grammar demands an indented statement stub.

```python
for n in range(1, 7):
    if n == 2:
        pass          # Placeholder: does nothing, falls through to print(2)
    if n == 4:
        continue      # Skips printing 4 only
    if n == 6:
        break         # Exits loop before printing 6
    print(n, end=" ") # Output: 1 2 3 5 
```

### (ii) Difference Between `list` and `dict` (2 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Python `list` vs `dict`
> | Parameter | `list` | `dict` (Dictionary) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Data Organization** | Ordered dynamic array of elements: `[70, 85, 92]`. | Hash-table mapping of `key: value` pairs: `{'roll': 1, 'score': 85}`. |
> | **Element Access & Complexity** | Zero-based integer offset `lst[i]` (`O(1)` index; `O(n)` value search `x in lst`). | Hashable key lookup `d[k]` (`O(1)` average lookup and `k in d`). |
> | **Duplicate Policy** | Duplicate values permitted at distinct indices. | Keys must be unique and immutable/hashable; values may repeat. |

### (iii) Python Program to Check Whether a Number Is Prime (3 Marks)

```python
def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n == 2:
        return True
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return False
    limit = int(n ** 0.5)
    for d in range(3, limit + 1, 2):
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
    return True


for val in [1, 2, 17, 21, 29]:
    print(f"{val:2d} -> {'Prime' if is_prime(val) else 'Not Prime'}")
# Output: 1 -> Not Prime | 2 -> Prime | 17 -> Prime | 21 -> Not Prime | 29 -> Prime
```

- **Trial-Division Logic:** Testing odd divisors up to `⌊√n⌋` runs in `O(√n)` time because any composite `n = a × b` must have `min(a, b) <= √n`.

### (i) Four Types of Function Arguments in Python (4 Marks)

1. **Positional (Required) Arguments:** Passed in exact left-to-right parameter order; omitting or swapping them changes semantics or raises `TypeError`.
2. **Keyword Arguments:** Passed explicitly as `param=value` at the call site, making call order flexible and self-documenting (must appear *after* positional arguments).
3. **Default Arguments:** Declared with a fallback value (`rate=5.0`) in the `def` header; used automatically whenever the caller omits that parameter.
4. **Variable-Length Arguments (`*args` and `**kwargs`):** `*args` packs arbitrary extra positional arguments into a **`tuple`**, whereas `**kwargs` packs arbitrary extra keyword arguments into a **`dict`**.

```python
def register(roll, dept="CST", *subjects, **meta):
    return f"Roll={roll}, Dept={dept}, Subjects={subjects}, Meta={meta}"

print(register(101))                                          # Default dept='CST'
print(register(dept="ETCE", roll=102))                        # Keyword arguments
print(register(103, "CST", "Python", "DS", sem=3, sec="A"))   # *args + **kwargs
# Output line 3: Roll=103, Dept=CST, Subjects=('Python', 'DS'), Meta={'sem': 3, 'sec': 'A'}
```

### (ii) Recursive Factorial Script (4 Marks)

> [!FORMULA] Factorial Recurrence Relation
> `n! = 1` if `n == 0` or `n == 1` (base case), and `n! = n × (n - 1)!` for integer `n >= 2`.

```python
def factorial(n: int) -> int:
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Factorial is undefined for negative integers")
    if n == 0 or n == 1:          # Base case terminates recursion
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # Recursive decomposition step


for k in [0, 1, 5, 6]:
    print(f"{k}! = {factorial(k)}")
# Verified Output: 0! = 1 | 1! = 1 | 5! = 120 | 6! = 720
```

- **Call-Stack Unwinding for `factorial(4)`:** `4 * factorial(3) -> 4 * (3 * factorial(2)) -> 4 * (3 * (2 * factorial(1))) -> 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24` (`O(n)` time and `O(n)` call-stack depth).

### (i) Module vs Package in Python with Examples (4 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Python Module vs Python Package
> | Parameter | Module | Package |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Physical Structure** | A **single `.py` file** containing definitions and statements. | A **directory** grouping multiple `.py` modules (plus optional `__init__.py` and sub-packages). |
> | **Namespace Level** | Single flat namespace (`import billing`). | Hierarchical dotted namespace (`from ecommerce.payments import upi`). |
> | **Primary Goal** | File-level code reuse within a feature. | Project/library-scale modular organization without module-name collisions. |

```python
# Module example: converter.py
def c_to_f(c):
    return (c * 9 / 5) + 32

# Package example: analytics/__init__.py + analytics/summary.py
# Imported via: from analytics import summary
```

### (ii) Global, Local, Class Scope, and Nonlocal Variables (4 Marks)

Python resolves unqualified identifiers via the **LEGB Rule** (**L**ocal → **E**nclosing → **G**lobal → **B**uilt-in), while class bodies form a dedicated attribute namespace:

- **Local Variable (`L`):** Assigned inside a `def` function; lives in that call frame's symbol table and disappears when the function returns.
- **Nonlocal / Enclosing Variable (`E`):** Bound in an outer enclosing function and mutated inside a nested inner function via `nonlocal var` (bridges closures without polluting module globals).
- **Global Variable (`G`):** Assigned at the top level of a `.py` module; readable anywhere in the module, and rebound from inside a function using `global var`.
- **Class Scope Variable:** Defined directly inside a `class` body (`college = "WBSCTE"`); shared across instances as `ClassName.attr` (note: methods do **not** resolve bare class names via LEGB — they access `self.attr` or `ClassName.attr`).

```python
tax_rate = 0.18                 # Global variable

class Invoice:
    currency = "INR"            # Class-scope attribute

def outer():
    count = 0                   # Enclosing variable
    def inner():
        nonlocal count          # Rebinds enclosing 'count'
        local_step = 1          # Local variable
        count += local_step
    inner()
    return count, Invoice.currency, tax_rate

print(outer())                  # Verified Output: (1, 'INR', 0.18)
```

### (i) `readline()` vs `readlines()` (3 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] `readline()` vs `readlines()`
> | Parameter | `f.readline()` | `f.readlines()` |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Amount Read** | Reads **at most one line** from the current file offset up to `'\n'`. | Reads **all remaining lines** until EOF in one call. |
> | **Return Type** | Single `str` (returns empty string `''` at EOF). | `list[str]` containing every remaining line (`[]` at EOF). |
> | **Memory Footprint** | `O(line_length)` — safe for multi-gigabyte log files. | `O(file_size)` — materializes the entire file in RAM. |

### (ii) `write()` vs `writelines()` (3 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] `write()` vs `writelines()`
> | Parameter | `f.write(s)` | `f.writelines(iterable)` |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Accepted Argument** | Exactly **one `str`** (or `bytes` in binary mode). | Any **iterable of strings** (`list`, `tuple`, generator). |
> | **Return Value** | Returns `int` count of characters/bytes written. | Returns `None`. |
> | **Newline Behaviour** | Does **not** append `'\n'` automatically. | Does **not** insert `'\n'` between items — caller supplies `'\n'`. |

### (iii) `open()` and `close()` (2 Marks)

- **`open(file, mode='r', encoding='utf-8')`:** Requests an OS file descriptor and returns a buffered Python stream object positioned at byte `0` (or EOF in `'a'` mode).
- **`f.close()`:** Flushes unwritten user-space buffers to disk and releases the OS file descriptor (`f.closed` becomes `True`); using `with open(...) as f:` guarantees `f.close()` runs automatically even if an exception occurs:

```python
with open("sample.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    count = f.write("Alpha\n")
    f.writelines(["Beta\n", "Gamma\n"])

with open("sample.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    first = f.readline()          # 'Alpha\n'
    rest = f.readlines()          # ['Beta\n', 'Gamma\n']
print(count, first.strip(), rest) # Output: 6 Alpha ['Beta\n', 'Gamma\n']
```

### (i) Python Program to Count Words in `file.txt` (4 Marks)

```python
def count_words(filepath: str = "file.txt") -> int:
    total_words = 0
    # Stream line-by-line so arbitrarily large files use O(1) memory
    with open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            total_words += len(line.split())
    return total_words


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        print("Number of words in file.txt:", count_words("file.txt"))
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("Error: file.txt does not exist in the working directory.")
```

- **How It Works:** `line.split()` (with no arguments) splits on runs of arbitrary whitespace (`' '`, `'\t'`, `'\n'`) and discards empty leading/trailing tokens, while `with open(...)` guarantees deterministic file closure.

### (ii) MVC Architectural Pattern (2 Marks)

- **Model:** Encapsulates data structures, database schema/ORM queries, and domain validation rules.
- **View:** Renders data into the user interface (HTML/JSON) without embedding database logic.
- **Controller:** Receives user HTTP requests, coordinates Model updates, and selects the View to return (in Django's **MVT** variant, Django's URL dispatcher + View act as Controller and Templates render HTML).

### (iii) Is Django Better Than Flask? (2 Marks)

Neither framework is universally "better" — each targets a different architectural trade-off:

> [!COMPARE] Django vs Flask Web Frameworks
> | Aspect | Django (Full-Stack "Batteries-Included") | Flask (Lightweight Micro-Framework) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Built-In Components** | Ships with ORM, migrations, Admin UI, auth, CSRF protection, and forms out of the box. | Ships with WSGI routing + Jinja2 templates; database/auth chosen via extensions (`SQLAlchemy`). |
> | **Best Fit** | Large database-backed portals, ERPs, CMSs, and rapid convention-driven team projects. | Lightweight REST microservices, prototypes, custom ML model APIs, and non-relational backends. |

### (i) The `range()` Function and Its Use in a `for` Loop (3 Marks)

- **Definition & Signatures:** `range(stop)`, `range(start, stop)`, or `range(start, stop, step)` returns an **immutable, lazy integer-sequence object** representing arithmetic progressions from `start` (inclusive, default `0`) up to `stop` (exclusive) by non-zero `step` (default `1`).
- **Constant-Memory Advantage:** Stores only `(start, stop, step)` in `O(1)` RAM regardless of whether `stop` is `10` or `10**9`, computing values on demand during `for` iteration:

```python
for num in range(2, 11, 2):
    print(num, end=" ")   # Verified Output: 2 4 6 8 10 
```

### (ii) Three Ways to Format Strings in Python (3 Marks)

1. **Formatted String Literals (`f-strings`, Python 3.6+):** Evaluates Python expressions inline inside `{...}` with optional format specifiers (`:.2f`) — fastest and most readable.
2. **`str.format()` Method:** Substitutes positional or named placeholders `{0}` / `{name}`.
3. **Printf-Style `%` Interpolation:** Legacy C-style `%s`, `%d`, `%.2f` tuple formatting.

```python
name, cgpa = "Ananya", 8.756
print(f"{name} achieved {cgpa:.2f} CGPA")               # 1. f-string
print("{} achieved {:.2f} CGPA".format(name, cgpa))     # 2. str.format()
print("%s achieved %.2f CGPA" % (name, cgpa))           # 3. %-formatting
# All three print: Ananya achieved 8.76 CGPA
```

### (iii) Classification into Mutable and Immutable Data Types (2 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] Mutable vs Immutable Built-In Data Types
> | Parameter | Mutable Data Types | Immutable Data Types |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Built-In Types** | `list`, `dict`, `set`, `bytearray` | `int`, `float`, `complex`, `bool`, `str`, `tuple`, `frozenset`, `bytes`, `range` |
> | **In-Place Modification** | Allowed — `id(obj)` stays identical after `append()` / item assignment. | Forbidden — operations allocate a brand-new object (`id` changes); item assignment raises `TypeError`. |
> | **Hashability** | Unhashable (`cannot be dict keys`). | Hashable (`valid as dict keys / set elements`, provided tuple items are hashable). |

### (i) `start()` and `end()` Methods on Regex `Match` Objects (2 Marks)

When `re.search()` or `re.match()` succeeds, it returns a `re.Match` object recording the exact slice indices of the matched substring (or capturing group `g`):
- **`m.start()`:** Zero-based starting index of the match in the target string.
- **`m.end()`:** Exclusive ending index (`1` past the last matched character), so `text[m.start():m.end()] == m.group()` (and `m.span()` returns `(m.start(), m.end())`).

```python
import re
text = "Exam code PY-307 starts"
m = re.search(r"PY-\d+", text)
print(m.start(), m.end(), text[m.start():m.end()])   # Output: 10 16 PY-307
```

### (ii) `re.match()`, `re.split()`, and `re.findall()` with Examples (3 Marks)

| Function | Matching Rule & Return Type | Example (`import re`) |
|---|---|---|
| `re.match(pat, s)` | Anchors strictly at **index `0`** (beginning of string); returns `Match` or `None`. | `re.match(r"\d+", "42abc").group() -> '42'` (`re.match(r"\d+", "x42") -> None`) |
| `re.split(pat, s)` | Splits `s` at every occurrence of regex delimiter `pat`; returns `list[str]`. | `re.split(r"[,;\s]+", "C, Python; DS") -> ['C', 'Python', 'DS']` |
| `re.findall(pat, s)` | Scans entire string left-to-right and returns all non-overlapping matches as `list[str]`. | `re.findall(r"\d+", "Q1: 8m, Q2: 10m") -> ['1', '8', '2', '10']` |

### (iii) Package for Fourier Transformation & Array Addition Program (3 Marks)

- **Package Name:** **NumPy** (`numpy`, specifically its `numpy.fft` Discrete/Fast Fourier Transform subpackage; `scipy.fft` builds on the same ecosystem).
- **Vectorized Array Addition & FFT Program:**

```python
import numpy as np

arr1 = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
arr2 = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])

# Element-wise vectorized addition (via '+' operator or np.add)
sum_arr = np.add(arr1, arr2)
print("Sum of arrays:", sum_arr)            # Output: [11 22 33 44]

# 1D Fast Fourier Transform via numpy.fft
signal = np.array([1.0, 0.0, -1.0, 0.0])
print("FFT spectrum:", np.fft.fft(signal))  # Output: [0.+0.j 2.+0.j 0.+0.j 2.+0.j]
```

### (a) Built-in Data Types in Python (5 Marks)

Python is dynamically and strongly typed: variables hold references to typed heap objects rather than fixed-type memory slots. Its standard built-in data types fall into seven core families:

| Category | Built-in Type(s) | Mutability | Representative Literal / Constructor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Numeric** | `int`, `float`, `complex` | Immutable | `42`, `3.14159`, `3 + 4j` |
| **Boolean** | `bool` (subclass of `int`) | Immutable | `True`, `False` |
| **Text Sequence** | `str` | Immutable | `'Python'`, `"Diploma"` |
| **Sequence Types** | `list` (mutable); `tuple`, `range` (immutable) | Mixed | `[10, 20]`, `(10, 20)`, `range(0, 10, 2)` |
| **Mapping** | `dict` | Mutable | `{'roll': 101, 'dept': 'CST'}` |
| **Set Types** | `set` (mutable); `frozenset` (immutable) | Mixed | `{1, 2, 3}`, `frozenset([1, 2])` |
| **Binary & Null** | `bytes`, `bytearray`, `memoryview`, `NoneType` | Mixed / Immutable | `b'ABC'`, `bytearray(4)`, `None` |

- **Arbitrary-Precision Integers:** Python `int` grows dynamically to arbitrary precision without 32-bit/64-bit integer overflow, while `float` follows IEEE-754 double precision.
- **Mutability & Hashing Rule:** Immutable objects (`int`, `str`, `tuple` of immutables, `frozenset`) are hashable and valid as `dict` keys or `set` members; mutable containers (`list`, `dict`, `set`) can be modified in place without changing `id(obj)`.

### (b) Importance of Indentation in Python (3 Marks)

- **Syntactic Block Delimiter:** Unlike C or Java (which delimit blocks with `{ ... }`), Python uses leading whitespace (**off-side rule**, PEP 8 standard = **4 spaces per level**) to group statements belonging to `if`, `for`, `while`, `def`, `class`, and `try` suites.
- **Compile-Time Enforcement:** Dedenting marks the end of a suite, while inconsistent or missing indentation raises `IndentationError` (or `TabError` when mixing tabs and spaces) before execution.
- **Semantic Impact:** Shifting a statement's indentation changes program logic directly:

```python
marks = 35
if marks >= 40:
    print("Passed")       # Inside the if-suite: skipped when marks == 35
    print("Congrats!")    # Same indentation level -> same block
print("Result Checked")   # Dedented: executes unconditionally
```

### (a) Representing a String in Python (3 Marks)

- **Unicode Sequence:** In Python 3, a string (`str`) is an **ordered, immutable sequence of Unicode code points**.
- **Four Quoting Forms:** Strings can be written using single quotes (`'...'`), double quotes (`"..."`), triple quotes (`'''...'''` or `"""..."""` for multi-line text and docstrings), or raw prefix `r'...'` (which disables backslash escape sequences like `\n`):

```python
s1 = 'Kolkata'                    # Single-quoted string
s2 = "Student's Copy"             # Double quotes allow embedded apostrophe
s3 = """Line 1
Line 2"""                         # Triple-quoted multi-line string
s4 = r'C:\new_folder\test.py'     # Raw string preserves backslashes literally
print(s1[0], s1[-1], s1[1:4])     # Output: K a olk
```

- **Immutability:** Individual characters can be read with zero-based (`s1[0]`) or negative (`s1[-1]`) indexing, but item assignment (`s1[0] = 'M'`) raises `TypeError`.

### (b) Python Program to Check Palindrome String (5 Marks)

A string is a **palindrome** if it reads identically forward and backward after normalizing case (for example, `"Madam"` or `"racecar"`).

```python
def is_palindrome(text: str) -> bool:
    cleaned = text.strip().lower()
    # Compare characters from both ends moving inward (O(n) time, O(1) index check)
    left, right = 0, len(cleaned) - 1
    while left < right:
        if cleaned[left] != cleaned[right]:
            return False
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return True


# Demonstration with idiomatic slice check s == s[::-1] alongside two-pointer check
for sample in ["Madam", "level", "Python"]:
    normalized = sample.lower()
    slice_check = (normalized == normalized[::-1])
    verdict = "Palindrome" if is_palindrome(sample) and slice_check else "Not a Palindrome"
    print(f"{sample!r:10} -> {verdict}")
```

- **Verified Output:**

```text
'Madam'    -> Palindrome
'level'    -> Palindrome
'Python'   -> Not a Palindrome
```

- **How It Works:** Both two-pointer inward comparison (`cleaned[left] == cleaned[right]`) and Python's step-`-1` slice reversal (`normalized == normalized[::-1]`) run in `O(n)` time over string length `n`.

### (a) Lists vs Tuples vs Dictionaries (5 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] List vs Tuple vs Dictionary in Python
> | Parameter | `list` | `tuple` | `dict` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **Literal Syntax** | Square brackets: `[10, 20, 30]` | Parentheses / comma: `(10, 20, 30)` | Curly braces `key: value`: `{'id': 10, 'gpa': 8.5}` |
> | **Mutability** | **Mutable** (append, pop, sort, assign in place). | **Immutable** (fixed size and element bindings). | **Mutable** mapping (insert, update, delete keys). |
> | **Access Mechanism** | Positional integer index (`0` to `n-1` or `-1`). | Positional integer index (`0` to `n-1` or `-1`). | Unique hashable key (`d['id']` or `d.get('id')`, `O(1)` average). |
> | **Duplicate Elements** | Allowed freely. | Allowed freely. | Keys must be unique (values may repeat). |
> | **Hashability & Dict Key Use** | Unhashable (`TypeError` if used as key). | Hashable if all contained items are hashable. | Unhashable (`TypeError` if used as key). |
> | **Typical Use Case** | Dynamic homogeneous/heterogeneous collections. | Fixed records, coordinates, multiple return values. | Fast key-based lookup tables and structured records. |

```python
marks = [78, 85, 91]          # List: mutable
marks[0] = 80                 # Valid -> [80, 85, 91]

coords = (22.57, 88.36)       # Tuple: immutable coordinate pair
student = {"roll": 7, "marks": marks, "loc": coords}
print(student["roll"], student["loc"][0])   # Output: 7 22.57
```

### (b) List Slicing vs List Indexing (3 Marks)

> [!COMPARE] List Indexing vs List Slicing
> | Aspect | List Indexing (`lst[i]`) | List Slicing (`lst[start:stop:step]`) |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Return Value** | Returns the **single element** stored at position `i` (unwrapped item type). | Always returns a **new `list`** containing the extracted subsequence (`[]` if empty). |
> | **Out-of-Range Behaviour** | Raises `IndexError` when `i >= len(lst)` or `i < -len(lst)`. | Clamps bounds gracefully without raising `IndexError` (`lst[2:99]` works safely). |
> | **Step & Reversal** | Accesses one offset only (`lst[-1]` = last item). | Supports arbitrary stride and reversal (`lst[::2]`, `lst[::-1]`). |

```python
a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(a[2], type(a[2]).__name__)       # Output: 30 int
print(a[1:4], a[::-1])                 # Output: [20, 30, 40] [50, 40, 30, 20, 10]
```
